description: We are Arz961, top 5 nominees in the 2025 NASA Space Apps Beirut challenge for the Hunting for Exoplanets with AI challenge. We are interested in software engineering and AI, which is why we chose the Flame in Freefall challenge for 2026.
summary: Flame in Freefall is an SI-powered web dashboard that turns NASA's scattered ISS fire experiments into clear, cited fire-safety answers for crews heading to the Moon and Mars. We cleaned 12 messy tables from NASA's PSI database (plus one NASA 1-g reference) into one table of 992 records. Users pick a habitat (ISS, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars, spacesuit) and the Habitat Risk Navigator ranks the most relevant investigations with a transparent score and shows where NASA has no data at all. A flame predictor estimates if a fuel droplet flame goes out and how fast it burns, with uncertainty. "Ask PSI", an AI agent, answers plain-English questions and cites the exact PSI id and DOI for every claim. The same data is also available inside any AI assistant through our MCP server. This matters because Moon habitats will run at 30%+ oxygen, where materials burn much more easily, and engineers need quick, trustworthy answers from the data NASA already has.
details:
What it does

  • One place for NASA's ISS fire tests: 992 records from 10 sources (780 flown tests, 160 planned FLEX-2 points, 52 ground 1-g thresholds), every number linked to its source.
  • 3D Explore view: real NASA imagery of Earth, Moon and Mars. Click a habitat to open its fire-risk panel.
  • Habitat Risk Navigator: presets for ISS (21% O2, 14.7 psi), Moon base (30% O2, 10.2 psi), pressurized rover, Mars, spacesuit (100% O2, 4.3 psi). Ranks investigations by closeness of oxygen, pressure, airflow and fuel, plus fire-safety pillar (prevention, detection, suppression). The weights are shown, so the ranking is explainable. A coverage map marks "No data here" where NASA never tested.
  • Compare investigations: hardware, fuels, conditions, sensors and results side by side, with what is shared and what differs.
  • Flame predictor: chance that a heptane or methanol droplet flame goes out by itself, and its burning-rate constant. Shows an uncertainty range, warns when inputs are outside the tested range, and draws the flame to scale.
  • Ask PSI: an AI agent that answers questions using only two tools, read-only SQL over the test table and a search over investigation descriptions, crew test notes and live NASA Technical Reports Server results. Every answer cites PSI id + DOI or NTRS id. Made-up links are detected and removed.
  • Unified test table: filter, search and download as CSV. Each row keeps its raw source file and a provenance flag.
  • Earth benefits: water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors that tell smoke from dust, firefighter breathing gear.
  • MCP server: 10 read-only tools (test table, SQL, navigator, compare, predictor, NASA reports) so Claude, Cursor or any MCP client can use our data with the same numbers and citations.

What we found in the data

  • More oxygen, faster burning: in FLEX, the average burning-rate constant rises from about 0.36 mm²/s at 12% O2 to about 0.71 mm²/s at 34% O2. A Moon base at 30% O2 sits at the high end.
  • Diluting the air helps put flames out: in FLEX, 57% of flames self-extinguished in nitrogen-diluted air, 72% with added CO2 and 80% with added helium.
  • NASA has fire data at 0 g and at 1 g, but none yet at Moon or Mars gravity. The dashboard says so instead of guessing, and uses 0 g and 1 g as bounds.

How it works

  1. Data pipeline (Python, pandas): reads the PSI experimental tables, fixes units typed inside cells, ranges, estimates ("~21.5"), notes mixed into data rows and broken column names, and maps everything to one schema (fuel, phase, O2, pressure, flow, diluent, outcome, metric). An LLM only drafts column mappings for new files. It never writes data values. Output: a SQLite database.
    • Extinction: logistic regression with interaction terms, 40-member bootstrap ensemble. AUC 0.88, Brier 0.079 (206 runs).
    • Burning rate: ridge regression, 40-member ensemble. R² 0.68, MAE 0.050 mm²/s (257 runs).
    • Both beat 14 alternatives we tested (random forest, boosting, SVM, kNN, neural nets).
  2. Services: FastAPI services for the models and the Ask PSI agent (LangGraph), plus an MCP server.
  3. Web app: Next.js 15, React 19, three.js for the 3D scene, Recharts for charts. Everything runs with one Docker Compose command.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Aerospace engineers can check in minutes whether a material or atmosphere was ever tested near their habitat conditions.
  • Researchers can compare investigations side by side and find the gaps NASA still needs to fill (partial gravity, high oxygen).
  • Students get a plain-English entry point into microgravity combustion, always with sources.
  • On Earth, the same science supports better extinguishers, smoke detectors and firefighter gear.

Tools and languages

Python, TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js, Recharts, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, HTTPX, LangGraph, LangChain, MCP Python SDK, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (comparison only), SQLite, JupyterLab, matplotlib, ImageMagick, Docker Compose. Groq hosts the open-weight Qwen language model.

  • Apollo 1 and Apollo 13 lessons learned: https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-1 and https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-13
  • 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: https://www.nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir/

  • NTRS, spacecraft fire detection requirements: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170000248/downloads/20170000248.pdf
  • NASA Glenn Combustion Module-2 summary: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20050215409/downloads/20050215409.pdf
